reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it combines Clash of Clans gameplay with a subscriber-milestone giveaway offering a $10 iTunes gift card for subscribing and liking. The requested actions are ordinary channel-engagement actions, and the title indicates that the giveaway is closed.

citations.quote: 300 SUBSCRIBERS! | $10 iTunes Gift Card Giveaway! [CLOSED]
To thank you all, I am doing a $10 iTunes gift card giveaway! All you have to do is to subscribe and like this video to be entered to win!
You have to do is subscribe and like and you'll be entered in automatically in one month from. The release date of this video.
So anyway, I'm going to show you a raid

opening.argument: The core offer is explicitly tied to viewer action: the video promises entry into a $10 iTunes gift-card giveaway in exchange for subscribing and liking. That is not merely discussion of a reward; it is a solicitation whose required actions are presented as sufficient for entry, with winner selection deferred for a month. The low-effort action and promised digital reward are the entire participation pathway, which makes this an easy-reward acquisition claim rather than ordinary gameplay alone.

citations.quote: All you have to do is to subscribe and like this video to be entered to win!
You have to do is subscribe and like and you'll be entered in automatically in one month from.
$10 iTunes Gift Card Giveaway!

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the requested actions ordinary engagement does not remove the linked reward. The description expressly makes subscribing and liking the condition for entry, while the gameplay is incidental to that offer. The word “closed” in the title does not establish that the promised card was awarded or that the solicitation was genuine; it only describes the stated status of the giveaway.

citations.quote: All you have to do is to subscribe and like this video to be entered to win!
[CLOSED]
I'm going to choose a winner and I will message you through the YouTube message

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The offer is a small promotional giveaway, not a claim that viewers can obtain an asset through a deceptive external claim process. The stated requirement is only subscribing and liking, and the speaker says a winner will be chosen and messaged; the evidence does not show that anyone paid, supplied credentials, or was denied a reward. The linkage alone therefore shows a promotion, not a scam.

citations.quote: it's free, the only thing. You have to do is subscribe and like
I'm going to choose a winner and I will message you through the YouTube message

opening.argument: Several risk signals are concentrated in a single pitch: the reward is a digital gift card, it is described as free, and entry is portrayed as automatic after only subscribing and liking. The title presents the offer as a subscriber milestone giveaway, while the description says similar gift-card giveaways recur at subscriber thresholds. That combination can create an unusually easy expectation of value in return for minimal engagement, without evidence in the supplied material that the stated prize was actually delivered.

citations.quote: $10 iTunes Gift Card Giveaway!
it's very easy to be entered, it's free
you'll be entered in automatically in one month from.
Every 100 subscribers (until 500 which I will do even more special giveaways), I do a gift card giveaway

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense isolates each signal and calls it routine, but the relevant question is their combination. “Free,” “automatically,” a digital gift card, and recurring threshold-based giveaways all reduce friction while encouraging further channel growth. The gameplay does not verify the promotion, and the title's closed-status notation does not prove delivery of the advertised prize.

citations.quote: it's very easy to be entered, it's free
you'll be entered in automatically in one month from.
Every 100 subscribers (until 500 which I will do even more special giveaways), I do a gift card giveaway
[CLOSED]

true_side_reply.rebuttal: These are ordinary features of a modest channel promotion, not evidence of deception. The material identifies a $10 prize, limits entry to subscribing and liking, and gives a one-month selection window. Nothing supplied shows fabricated winners, payment demands, hidden conditions, or a failed delivery, so the risk signals do not establish scam conduct.

citations.quote: $10 iTunes Gift Card Giveaway!
the only thing. You have to do is subscribe and like
in around one month after this video

opening.argument: Although the video is framed around a Clash of Clans raid, that framing functions as promotional packaging for the subscriber drive. The speaker introduces the gift-card giveaway before showing the raid, repeats that subscribing and liking are the way to enter, and closes by repeating the same instruction. The gameplay supplies attention and entertainment, but the recurring call to action steers viewers toward participation in the easy-reward offer.

citations.quote: today,. As you can see, I'm doing the $10 iTunes gift card giveaway for the 300 subscriber special.
So anyway, I'm going to show you a raid
Remember the way you can be entered is remember to like and subscribe and that is it. Free.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The presence of a raid does not neutralize the promotional function. The speaker announces the giveaway first, postpones the raid as a separate segment, and repeats the engagement instruction at the end. Describing the video as gameplay therefore omits the repeated reward-linked steering that supplies the reason to subscribe and like.

citations.quote: today,. As you can see, I'm doing the $10 iTunes gift card giveaway for the 300 subscriber special.
So anyway, I'm going to show you a raid
Remember the way you can be entered is remember to like and subscribe and that is it. Free.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A mixed video can contain both a legitimate promotion and gameplay without becoming a scam. The raid is explicitly shown as the video's substantive content, while the giveaway is described as thanks for reaching 300 subscribers. Repeating the entry instruction makes the promotion clear; it does not show deception, payment, or an exploitative claim pathway.
